idiom_name: trait with a provided (default) method as the skeleton + required methods as the steps
implementation_notes: A trait's provided (default) method is the pattern in the language's own vocabulary: the trait fixes the sequence, required methods are the primitive operations and default methods are the hooks - the Rust book introduces traits as shared behaviour that may come with default implementations, and Refactoring.guru's Rust realization writes the whole skeleton as a provided method. It replaces the abstract class entirely: no inheritance, no vtable unless you ask for one, static dispatch through generics or impl Trait and dynamic dispatch through dyn Trait. Because any implementor may also override a provided method, an invariant-bearing skeleton belongs in a concrete wrapper type or free function that takes the steps as a trait bound; the trait form is for the case where the sequence is a convenience rather than a guarantee.
pitfalls: A provided method can always be overridden by an implementor, so the skeleton is not final: put the invariant in a concrete wrapper or free function when it must not be bypassed.
A step taking &mut self, returning Self or using generics loses dyn-compatibility, so a skeleton meant to run behind Box<dyn Trait> must keep its methods object-safe.
Default methods cannot see the implementing type's private fields: a hook that needs state must reach it through required accessor methods, or the trait must be written in terms of associated types.
